Problem statement:
Diffusion models are widely used for generative tasks across domains. Given a pre-trained diffusion model, it is often desirable to fine-tune it further, either to align it with a downstream application or to correct errors that remain from imperfect learning.

Pre-trained generative models are commonly adapted to a task using reward feedback, and a standard strategy is to apply reinforcement learning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to a KL-regularized objective: maximize the expected reward while penalizing the KL divergence between the fine-tuned distribution and the distribution of the pre-trained (reference) model, whose optimum is the reference distribution tilted by the exponentiated reward. While such methods have found great success for language models, their adoption for diffusion models is not straightforward. Unlike autoregressive models, for which the marginal likelihood of a sample is easy to compute, diffusion models only give access to the conditional likelihoods of the successive denoising steps along the sampling trajectory, so the marginal KL divergence required for the regularization is intractable. In practice, the KL regularization is therefore either ignored or replaced by relaxations such as a KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories, which upper-bounds the marginal KL. Ignoring the KL term results in unstable training in large-scale settings, whereas the trajectory KL constraint gives subpar results and suffers from the initial value function bias problem: since the regularization is taken with respect to the learned reverse process, an appropriate tilt must be learned even for the distribution of the initial noise.

Apart from policy gradient methods, recent research has also studied fine-tuning based on rejection sampling, which keeps only high-reward samples generated by the model and trains on them (for example RSO, RAFT and Reinforce-Rej), as well as fine-tuning based on Best-of-N sampling and its relation to policy gradient methods. These approaches have mostly been developed and analyzed for autoregressive models, and how they relate to KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models, where marginal likelihoods are intractable, is not well understood.

Diffusion and flow models also have structure that methods designed for autoregressive models do not use: a sample is produced by progressively transforming Gaussian noise through a sequence of intermediate noisy states, either along a stochastic denoising process or, for flow models, along a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE). How this structure can be leveraged to make fine-tuning more effective is an open question.

Finally, adaptation is not always driven by an explicit reward. Because of the discretization error of the sampling ODE and the statistical error of imperfect learning, the distribution generated by a pre-trained flow model differs from the target data distribution. Whether such errors can be corrected after pre-training, using only samples from the data distribution and no explicit reward, and without a large increase in the compute needed per generated sample, is likewise open.

This leads to the following questions. How can a diffusion model be fine-tuned towards a reward under a principled KL regularization towards the pre-trained model when the marginal likelihoods needed for this regularization are intractable? Can the multi-step generative structure of diffusion and flow models be exploited to make such fine-tuning more effective? And can the errors of a pre-trained flow model be corrected without any explicit reward, improving sample quality at a reasonable cost in generation compute?

TITLE: Iterated rejection sampling as KL-regularised reward fine-tuning for diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We show that repeatedly fine-tuning a diffusion model on its own reward-filtered samples, where each round accepts a sample with probability proportional to the exponentiated reward divided by a running bound, converges to the reference distribution tilted by the reward, so the marginal KL term never has to be evaluated. We test this on a latent text-to-image model with an aesthetic reward and on a molecule generator with a docking proxy, tracking reward, sample diversity and a held-out estimate of KL from importance weights.

COST: 640
PREDICTION: Reward should rise steadily while diversity stays close to the reference model, unlike the unregularised baseline. The guarantee may break when the acceptance rate falls too low for steep rewards.

TITLE: Splitting the denoising chain into stages for reward fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a pretrained diffusion model one segment of the sampling trajectory at a time, starting from the final denoising steps and moving backwards, so that each stage solves a short-horizon KL-regularised problem whose solution is the previous stage tilted by an intermediate reward estimate. The intermediate rewards come from a learned value model on noisy states. We evaluate on text-to-image alignment with a preference reward and on layout generation with a constraint-satisfaction reward.
CONTROLS: We compare against fine-tuning all steps jointly with the same reward, against a version without the value model that propagates the final reward directly, and against the frozen reference model, reporting reward, Fréchet distance and an importance-weighted KL estimate for each.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Staged fine-tuning should reach the joint method's reward with fewer reward queries and less drift from the reference. If the value model on noisy states is poor, early stages will tilt toward the wrong regions and the advantage will vanish.

TITLE: Reward tilting through noise-level importance resampling
PROPOSAL: We treat each intermediate noisy state of a diffusion sampler as a particle and resample particles at several noise levels according to a look-ahead reward estimate, then fine-tune the model on the resulting trajectories. Because the resampling weights telescope, the fine-tuned model targets the reward-tilted reference distribution without needing marginal likelihoods. We apply it to an open latent diffusion model trained on public image-text pairs and to a graph diffusion model for small molecules scored by a drug-likeness reward.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning on final-step resampling only, sequential Monte Carlo at inference with no fine-tuning, and trajectory-penalised policy gradient, compared on reward, diversity and estimated divergence.
COST: 760
PREDICTION: Intermediate resampling should reach a given reward with less divergence than final-step resampling. Weight degeneracy at high noise levels could erase the benefit for sharp rewards.

Problem statement:
Diffusion models are widely used for generative tasks across domains. Given a pre-trained diffusion model, it is often desirable to fine-tune it further, either to align it with a downstream application or to correct errors that remain from imperfect learning.

Pre-trained generative models are commonly adapted to a task using reward feedback, and a standard strategy is to apply reinforcement learning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to a KL-regularized objective: maximize the expected reward while penalizing the KL divergence between the fine-tuned distribution and the distribution of the pre-trained (reference) model, whose optimum is the reference distribution tilted by the exponentiated reward. While such methods have found great success for language models, their adoption for diffusion models is not straightforward. Unlike autoregressive models, for which the marginal likelihood of a sample is easy to compute, diffusion models only give access to the conditional likelihoods of the successive denoising steps along the sampling trajectory, so the marginal KL divergence required for the regularization is intractable. In practice, the KL regularization is therefore either ignored or replaced by relaxations such as a KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories, which upper-bounds the marginal KL. Ignoring the KL term results in unstable training in large-scale settings, whereas the trajectory KL constraint gives subpar results and suffers from the initial value function bias problem: since the regularization is taken with respect to the learned reverse process, an appropriate tilt must be learned even for the distribution of the initial noise.

Apart from policy gradient methods, recent research has also studied fine-tuning based on rejection sampling, which keeps only high-reward samples generated by the model and trains on them (for example RSO, RAFT and Reinforce-Rej), as well as fine-tuning based on Best-of-N sampling and its relation to policy gradient methods. Problem statement:
Federated learning enables a group of users to collaboratively train models while preserving privacy, because local data never leave the users. Most conventional federated learning algorithms assume that users share the same model architecture or perform the same task, which limits their applicability in diverse real-world settings. Practical deployments may instead involve users with heterogeneous model architectures and different tasks, each with its own task-specific local dataset. For example, with recent advances in foundation models, a user can select a pre-trained foundation model according to its resource constraints (storage, communication and computation) and its task requirements, and then fine-tune it on a small local dataset. Task heterogeneity has motivated federated multi-task learning, whose goal is to let each user obtain a customized model for its own task while, under the orchestration of a server, capturing common task-agnostic information from the other users, so that every model generalizes better than if it were trained solely on its local data.

Early federated multi-task learning methods focused on personalization, i.e., non-IID data across users, and learned a customized model with the same architecture for every user. More recent methods address a wider range of tasks by dividing each model into a shared encoder and task-specific predictors. Consequently, most existing methods assume model congruity: users must employ fully or partially homogeneous architectures so that parameters can be shared. This prevents users from choosing arbitrary architectures, and revealing local model parameters also weakens privacy protection, particularly when users fine-tune pre-trained foundation models. Approaches designed for model heterogeneity have their own limitations. Methods in which each local model is a subset of a global model restrict the users' freedom to choose architectures. Knowledge-distillation-based methods that exchange outputs on an unlabeled public dataset accept arbitrary architectures, but knowledge can only be transferred among models with the same logit size, that is, among models solving the same task. A model-agnostic alternative adds a proximal term based on centered kernel alignment between representation matrices, but the reliability of this similarity measure is still under investigation. Federated semi-supervised methods that collaboratively pseudo-label a public dataset mostly handle only personalization tasks, and federated contrastive methods either assume homogeneous models or rely on class-wise prototypes, which makes them inapplicable to multi-task settings.

A related difficulty concerns learning a shared representation space across more than two models. Contrastive learning is a widely used technique for this purpose: it brings representations of the same instance (positives) closer together while pushing those of different instances (negatives) apart. The popular InfoNCE loss aligns the representations of two models; with more than two models, prior work typically applies InfoNCE to every pair of models. Such pairwise alignment, however, cannot effectively capture the dependencies among the representations obtained from all models. A recently proposed Gramian-based contrastive loss aligns all representations simultaneously, but it lacks theoretical justification. In multi-modal federated learning, which also relies on representation learning, one of the most effective methods aligns modalities through heuristic contrastive regularization and aggregation schemes that are difficult to extend beyond two modalities.

These gaps raise the following questions. How can users with heterogeneous model architectures and different tasks, possibly in different modalities, collaboratively improve their customized models, transferring knowledge across tasks without sharing local data and without requiring any architectural congruity? How can representations produced by an arbitrary number of models be aligned jointly, in a theoretically grounded way that captures the dependencies among all of them rather than only between pairs? And how can such collaboration remain practical and communication-efficient?

TITLE: Federated multi-task learning through a shared public-data representation space
PROPOSAL: We let each user keep an arbitrary encoder and task head, and coordinate only through embeddings of a small unlabelled public dataset that every user computes locally and sends to the server. TITLE: A volume-based contrastive loss for aligning many models at once
PROPOSAL: We propose a contrastive objective that treats the embeddings of one instance from all models as the columns of a matrix and rewards small volume of that matrix for positives relative to negatives, and we derive it as a lower bound on the total correlation among all representations. Early federated multi-task learning methods focused on personalization, i.e., non-IID data across users, and learned a customized model with the same architecture for every user. More recent methods address a wider range of tasks by dividing each model into a shared encoder and task-specific predictors. Consequently, most existing methods assume model congruity: users must employ fully or partially homogeneous architectures so that parameters can be shared. This prevents users from choosing arbitrary architectures, and revealing local model parameters also weakens privacy protection, particularly when users fine-tune pre-trained foundation models. Approaches designed for model heterogeneity have their own limitations. Methods in which each local model is a subset of a global model restrict the users' freedom to choose architectures. A model-agnostic alternative adds a proximal term based on centered kernel alignment between representation matrices, but the reliability of this similarity measure is still under investigation. Problem statement:
Accurate and dense semantic understanding of dynamic scenes is a critical capability for autonomous systems, including self-driving cars, drones, and robots. The prevalent paradigm, however, relies on conventional RGB cameras that capture information at discrete, often low, frequencies (e.g., 20 Hz). This low sampling rate creates significant "perceptual gaps", or "blind spots", between frames, during which fast-moving or abruptly appearing objects are not perceived, posing a severe risk in high-speed scenarios. Consider a pedestrian who suddenly enters a vehicle's path: at one frame time, a low-frame-rate system detects no hazard; when the pedestrian appears in the next frame, it may already be too late for the autonomous system to react. This motivates high-frame-rate perception that can produce reliable predictions at any moment in time. High-speed RGB cameras could mitigate this gap, but their prohibitive cost, high power consumption, and massive data bandwidth requirements make them impractical for scalable, real-world deployment.

Event cameras, in contrast, record brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution and with high dynamic range, naturally capturing high-temporal-resolution motion while consuming far less power and bandwidth. However, an event camera is temporally dense but spatially sparse, which limits its semantic information: event-only semantic segmentation methods often struggle to produce dense, high-fidelity semantic maps. An RGB camera cooperating with an event stream therefore offers a more practical and scalable way to build high-frame-rate perception.

The problem is then to predict a dense semantic map at any arbitrary timestamp $t+\delta t$ within the perceptual gap $(t, t+\Delta t]$ between two consecutive low-frame-rate frames, given only the initial RGB frame $I_t$ and the corresponding event stream $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$. Two constraints differentiate this setting from standard paradigms: causality (no future frame such as $I_{t+\Delta t}$ may be used) and anytime prediction (a prediction must be produced for any offset $\delta t \in (0, \Delta t]$, not just at fixed frame times). Existing paradigms fail one or both of these constraints. Video semantic segmentation methods leverage temporal coherence to improve segmentation consistency and efficiency across frames, but they are fundamentally frame-based and presuppose a dense, high-frame-rate RGB video stream as input. Video interpolation and related approaches that transfer information between two known RGB frames require the future frame and are therefore non-causal. Multi-modal RGB-event fusion methods are designed for enhancement, that is, using past events to improve the segmentation of the RGB frame at time $t$ itself; they do not predict into the blind interval that follows a single frame and are therefore not anytime-capable.

This task presents a non-trivial challenge: how can the rich, static semantic context of a single past RGB frame be effectively merged with the temporally dense, but spatially sparse and often noisy, event stream, so that dense predictions remain accurate at an arbitrary target time? The difficulty is compounded in highly dynamic scenes and over long prediction intervals, where objects move, appear, or become occluded after the last frame was captured. More broadly, the question is whether reliable high-frame-rate semantic perception can be obtained from low-frame-rate RGB hardware, decoupling perceptual frequency from the sensor's frame rate.

TITLE: Anytime semantic segmentation by warping a past frame's features with event-derived motion
PROPOSAL: We encode the last RGB frame into dense semantic features once, estimate a continuous-time motion field from the event stream up to the query time with a recurrent event encoder conditioned on the target offset, and warp the frame features to that time before a light decoder predicts the semantic map. Only past and current events are used, so the method is causal, and the offset input makes it answer at any time inside the interval. We evaluate on driving datasets with paired events and labels, synthesising intermediate labels by interpolation where needed.

PREDICTION: Accuracy should decay slowly with offset and stay well above the copied segmentation at long offsets. Newly appearing objects not visible in the last frame may be missed.

Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) such as Llama, Mixtral and Qwen are evolving rapidly and are increasingly adopted in a wide range of applications. However, their autoregressive generation process, in which tokens are produced one at a time, combined with their massive parameter counts, leads to substantial inference latency and high computational cost. Speculative decoding has emerged as a highly effective and widely adopted way to mitigate this bottleneck without compromising the quality of the generated text: a smaller, faster draft model proposes a sequence of future tokens, which the larger target model then verifies in parallel, reducing the number of expensive forward passes of the target model while keeping the output identical to that of standard decoding (lossless acceleration).

Standard speculative decoding introduces a new burden, however: a separate draft model has to be trained and maintained, which demands additional training data and compute as well as careful tuning to keep the draft model compatible with the target model. Self-speculative decoding removes the external draft model by deriving draft predictions from the target model itself, for instance by skipping some layers or blocks, exiting early from intermediate layers, using efficient attention, Jacobi-style parallel decoding or lower-precision activations, or by reusing the target model's hidden states with lightweight draft heads. The self-speculative methods that reach the largest speedups (for example EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA or LayerSkip) still require dedicated training, typically for several days on a node of eight server GPUs such as the Nvidia A100. Training-free, on-the-fly self-speculative methods such as Lookahead decoding or SWIFT can be integrated seamlessly into existing models, but their acceleration is limited: they can fall short even of minimal retrieval-based drafting methods such as prompt lookup decoding, which simply reuse repeated n-grams from the context to propose draft tokens and are therefore inherently lightweight and universally applicable. This leaves a trade-off between speed and ease of use.

Cascade speculative decoding is a potential way out of this trade-off. Draft models are commonly autoregressive LLMs themselves, so they can in turn be accelerated by speculative decoding; applying this idea recursively with several draft models ordered by decreasing size and latency gives a vertical (also called hierarchical or multi-level) cascade. In addition, because rejecting a draft token discards all the draft tokens that follow it, early draft tokens matter more than later ones, which motivates a horizontal cascade that drafts the first tokens with a slower but more accurate model and subsequent tokens with progressively faster ones. Prior analysis of such cascades, which models the expected walltime improvement of speculative decoding as a function of each draft model's expected acceptance rate and of its cost relative to the target model, establishes provable improvements over standard speculative decoding, and shows that adding a retrieval-based statistical drafter of negligible cost at the bottom of the hierarchy can almost always bring further speedup. Yet cascades have so far relied on a family of separately trained draft models of decreasing size, which most LLMs do not have; requiring several distinct draft models makes cascade speculative decoding largely impractical for widespread adoption in real-world systems.

This raises the question of whether the benefits of cascading can be obtained without training any draft model. Training-free self-speculative techniques could in principle supply the intermediate levels of a cascade above a cheap retrieval-based drafter, but nothing guarantees that such a cascade is faster than speculative decoding with the retrieval-based drafter alone: an intermediate draft model only pays off if its acceptance rate is high enough relative to its cost, and the outcome may also depend on scheduling choices such as the draft length at each level and the number of cascade rounds. Moreover, the space of possible cascade configurations (which draft model to use, when to switch between draft models, and how many tokens each should draft) is large, and the acceptance rates and costs of self-derived draft models depend on the acceleration technique and on the hardware, and can vary across tasks and even within a single sequence, so cascade schedules with fixed hyperparameters may leave much of the potential unused.

Two research questions follow. First, can existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods be used to construct an effective cascade of draft models above retrieval-based drafting methods for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding? Second, can further speedup be achieved by adaptively choosing, during inference, which draft model to use and how many tokens to draft, with regard to the characteristics of the different self-speculative acceleration techniques?

Cascade speculative decoding is a potential way out of this trade-off. Draft models are commonly autoregressive LLMs themselves, so they can in turn be accelerated by speculative decoding; applying this idea recursively with several draft models ordered by decreasing size and latency gives a vertical (also called hierarchical or multi-level) cascade. TITLE: Fitting an analytical walltime model to self-derived drafters to predict cascade speedup
PROPOSAL: We characterise each training-free drafter by two measured quantities, its per-token acceptance rate against the target and its latency relative to one target forward pass, and we plug them into the expected-walltime model of cascade speculative decoding to predict the speedup of every two-level and three-level arrangement of Lookahead, SWIFT-style layer skipping, Jacobi iteration and prompt lookup. We then run the arrangements the model ranks best and worst on Llama-2-7B-chat and Mistral-7B-instruct across Spec-Bench and compare predicted with realised speedup. We optimise draft lengths per level under the model before measuring, so that the comparison is between the model's recommendation and its own expectation.
CONTROLS: Prompt lookup alone and autoregressive decoding give the floor, a brute-force grid over draft lengths for the best arrangement gives the ceiling, and we test the model's independence assumption by measuring the correlation of acceptance between consecutive draft positions. Latency is measured repeatedly per configuration and outputs are checked against greedy decoding.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: We expect the ranking of arrangements to be predicted correctly but the absolute speedup to be predicted too high for layer-skipping drafters, whose acceptance decays along the block. A large gap between the model's optimum and the grid optimum would mean that fixed-rate modelling is too coarse for self-derived drafters.

TITLE: Online draft-length control from recent acceptance in a two-level cascade

TITLE: Verifying two training-free drafts in one batched target pass
PROPOSAL: Instead of choosing a drafter in advance, we let prompt lookup and a layer-skipping self-draft each propose a block for the same position, and we verify both blocks in a single batched forward pass of the target, keeping whichever block yields the longer accepted prefix. The choice is therefore made after the fact at every round, at the price of a doubled verification batch, which on memory-bound decoding adds little latency. CONTROLS: We compare against each drafter alone with swept draft length, against the two-level cascade of the same drafters, against an oracle that picks the better block without paying for the batched pass, and against autoregressive decoding. Outputs are checked against greedy decoding and timings repeated, including the batched pass alone to measure its overhead.

PREDICTION: We expect the batched verification to beat each drafter alone on every category and to beat the cascade on chat and reasoning, where the lookup block is often empty. If the batched pass takes more than a fifth longer than a single pass, the gain vanishes on the smaller model.

TITLE: Three-level cascade with reduced-precision drafting above lookup
PROPOSAL: We build a three-level vertical cascade for Llama-3-8B-instruct and Llama-2-13B-chat: the target in full precision verifies a draft produced by the same weights run with eight-bit activations and weights, that reduced-precision copy is drafted by a layer-skipping self-draft of the reduced-precision copy, and the bottom level is prompt lookup. No level is trained, and only the target's verification determines the output. We measure walltime speedup over autoregressive decoding on Spec-Bench and on a long-form summarisation set, and we vary the number of cascade rounds the lower levels run before handing a block upward.
CONTROLS: Every two-level sub-cascade and each single-level method is run with swept draft lengths, so that the gain of adding each level is isolated; autoregressive decoding and lookup alone give the floor; the reduced-precision copy used as the only drafter checks that quantisation does not degrade acceptance below the useful range. Outputs are compared token by token with greedy decoding and timings repeated.
COST: 88
PREDICTION: We expect the reduced-precision level to accept almost every token but to save too little latency per token to pay for itself on the fastest card, and the full three-level cascade to beat the best two-level one only when lower levels run a single round. If the quantised copy accepts under ninety percent of tokens, the arrangement is dominated by the two-level cascade without it.

Problem statement:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a pivotal technique for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and intentions. As a critical component of this process, the reward model is trained to assign scores that quantify the degree of alignment between a model's outputs and human preferences. Well-designed reward signals, whether applied during training or at inference time (for example, to select the best among several sampled candidates), can significantly enhance LLM performance across diverse domains. However, learning a reward model that accurately captures human preference signals remains a significant challenge, and the two dominant paradigms both exhibit inherent limitations that hinder their effectiveness in practice.

Discriminative reward models append an MLP-based value head to a base model and are commonly optimized with the Bradley-Terry objective, which maximizes the score margin between chosen and rejected responses, to output a single scalar reward. Considerable research has improved this family through better data and refined modeling frameworks (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, and quantile- or uncertainty-based variants), yet these models remain limited to learning a pairwise ranking. Their scores are unbounded and uncalibrated, reflect only relative preferences rather than intrinsic quality, and lack a probabilistic interpretation: they indicate that one response is preferred over another, but not why, nor how good either response is in absolute terms. This makes it difficult to establish a trusted acceptance threshold that separates high-quality responses from low-quality ones. A single deterministic score per response also cannot express the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments: annotators often disagree, and inconsistent preference data is known to degrade reward model performance, yet such ambiguity is collapsed into a point estimate.

Generative reward models instead leverage the native generative capabilities of LLMs to produce chain-of-thought critiques before rendering a preference judgment, in line with the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, and recent reasoning-based variants trained with reinforcement learning show promising scalability in inference-time computation. While their critiques offer superior interpretability, they often rely on rigid pairwise input formats that limit flexibility in Best-of-N scenarios, where many candidates must be scored; they often struggle to outperform discriminative models under computational constraints; and achieving performance comparable to discriminative models frequently requires costly pointwise supervision for calibration, substantially increasing the annotation burden.

Consequently, the field faces a critical trade-off between the efficiency of discriminative reward models and the interpretability of generative ones, with neither offering a complete solution. This raises several open questions. Can a reward model match the efficiency and accuracy of discriminative models, score single or multiple responses flexibly, and still provide interpretable, calibrated scores with a meaningful measure of confidence? Can its scores reflect the absolute quality of a response, so that a fixed threshold reliably distinguishes good responses from bad ones, rather than encoding only relative rankings? Can it capture the uncertainty and annotator disagreement present in preference data instead of discarding them? And since absolute quality judgments are expensive to annotate at scale while pairwise preference data is comparatively abundant, how can a reward model be grounded in an absolute quality scale using only limited quality annotations, for instance when adapting it to a new domain, without sacrificing ranking accuracy?

Data type: Real-world data only
Experimental domains: LLM reward modeling for RLHF alignment, chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, code generation, chatbot safety, role-play dialogue

TITLE: A discrete quality distribution head trained from pairwise preferences
PROPOSAL: We replace the scalar value head of a discriminative reward model with a head that outputs a categorical distribution over five quality levels, and we train it on pairwise data from Skywork-Reward-Preference and HelpSteer2 with a Bradley-Terry likelihood applied to the expected level of each response, plus an entropy term that keeps the distribution from collapsing. Problem statement:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a pivotal technique for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and intentions. As a critical component of this process, the reward model is trained to assign scores that quantify the degree of alignment between a model's outputs and human preferences. Well-designed reward signals, whether applied during training or at inference time (for example, to select the best among several sampled candidates), can significantly enhance LLM performance across diverse domains. However, learning a reward model that accurately captures human preference signals remains a significant challenge, and the two dominant paradigms both exhibit inherent limitations that hinder their effectiveness in practice.

Discriminative reward models append an MLP-based value head to a base model and are commonly optimized with the Bradley-Terry objective, which maximizes the score margin between chosen and rejected responses, to output a single scalar reward. Considerable research has improved this family through better data and refined modeling frameworks (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, and quantile- or uncertainty-based variants), yet these models remain limited to learning a pairwise ranking. Their scores are unbounded and uncalibrated, reflect only relative preferences rather than intrinsic quality, and lack a probabilistic interpretation: they indicate that one response is preferred over another, but not why, nor how good either response is in absolute terms. This makes it difficult to establish a trusted acceptance threshold that separates high-quality responses from low-quality ones. A single deterministic score per response also cannot express the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments: annotators often disagree, and inconsistent preference data is known to degrade reward model performance, yet such ambiguity is collapsed into a point estimate.

Generative reward models instead leverage the native generative capabilities of LLMs to produce chain-of-thought critiques before rendering a preference judgment, in line with the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, and recent reasoning-based variants trained with reinforcement learning show promising scalability in inference-time computation. While their critiques offer superior interpretability, they often rely on rigid pairwise input formats that limit flexibility in Best-of-N scenarios, where many candidates must be scored; they often struggle to outperform discriminative models under computational constraints; and achieving performance comparable to discriminative models frequently requires costly pointwise supervision for calibration, substantially increasing the annotation burden.

Consequently, the field faces a critical trade-off between the efficiency of discriminative reward models and the interpretability of generative ones, with neither offering a complete solution. This raises several open questions. Can a reward model match the efficiency and accuracy of discriminative models, score single or multiple responses flexibly, and still provide interpretable, calibrated scores with a meaningful measure of confidence? Can its scores reflect the absolute quality of a response, so that a fixed threshold reliably distinguishes good responses from bad ones, rather than encoding only relative rankings? Can it capture the uncertainty and annotator disagreement present in preference data instead of discarding them? And since absolute quality judgments are expensive to annotate at scale while pairwise preference data is comparatively abundant, how can a reward model be grounded in an absolute quality scale using only limited quality annotations, for instance when adapting it to a new domain, without sacrificing ranking accuracy?

TITLE: Beta-distributed rewards that carry annotator disagreement
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head that outputs the two shape parameters of a Beta distribution over the quality of a response on the unit interval. TITLE: Ordinal thresholds anchor pairwise rewards to an absolute scale
PROPOSAL: We model response quality as a latent scalar from a reward head and learn a set of ordered cut points that map the latent to five quality bins, as in cumulative-link ordinal regression. Pairwise preference pairs train the latent through a Bradley-Terry likelihood, and a small set of pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2 trains the cut points and a single affine map of the latent, so that the abundant pairwise data fixes the ranking and the scarce absolute data fixes the scale. We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-instruct on Skywork-Reward-Preference for the pairwise part, vary the number of pointwise ratings from a few dozen to the full set, and evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench, bin accuracy against held-out ratings, and the precision of a fixed acceptance threshold on chat, mathematics and code candidates.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head with scores standardised per domain, the same head followed by Platt scaling on the pointwise ratings, a head trained on pointwise ratings alone, and cut points fitted to shuffled ratings as placebo, each over three seeds.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect the ranking accuracy to stay unchanged while bin accuracy rises steeply with the first hundred ratings and then saturates. Threshold precision should transfer across domains better than for standardised scalar scores, which fail where the domain mean shifts.

As a critical component of this process, the reward model is trained to assign scores that quantify the degree of alignment between a model's outputs and human preferences. Well-designed reward signals, whether applied during training or at inference time (for example, to select the best among several sampled candidates), can significantly enhance LLM performance across diverse domains. However, learning a reward model that accurately captures human preference signals remains a significant challenge, and the two dominant paradigms both exhibit inherent limitations that hinder their effectiveness in practice.

Discriminative reward models append an MLP-based value head to a base model and are commonly optimized with the Bradley-Terry objective, which maximizes the score margin between chosen and rejected responses, to output a single scalar reward. Considerable research has improved this family through better data and refined modeling frameworks (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, and quantile- or uncertainty-based variants), yet these models remain limited to learning a pairwise ranking. Their scores are unbounded and uncalibrated, reflect only relative preferences rather than intrinsic quality, and lack a probabilistic interpretation: they indicate that one response is preferred over another, but not why, nor how good either response is in absolute terms. This makes it difficult to establish a trusted acceptance threshold that separates high-quality responses from low-quality ones. A single deterministic score per response also cannot express the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments: annotators often disagree, and inconsistent preference data is known to degrade reward model performance, yet such ambiguity is collapsed into a point estimate.

Generative reward models instead leverage the native generative capabilities of LLMs to produce chain-of-thought critiques before rendering a preference judgment, in line with the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, and recent reasoning-based variants trained with reinforcement learning show promising scalability in inference-time computation. While their critiques offer superior interpretability, they often rely on rigid pairwise input formats that limit flexibility in Best-of-N scenarios, where many candidates must be scored; they often struggle to outperform discriminative models under computational constraints; and achieving performance comparable to discriminative models frequently requires costly pointwise supervision for calibration, substantially increasing the annotation burden.

Consequently, the field faces a critical trade-off between the efficiency of discriminative reward models and the interpretability of generative ones, with neither offering a complete solution. This raises several open questions. Can a reward model match the efficiency and accuracy of discriminative models, score single or multiple responses flexibly, and still provide interpretable, calibrated scores with a meaningful measure of confidence? Can its scores reflect the absolute quality of a response, so that a fixed threshold reliably distinguishes good responses from bad ones, rather than encoding only relative rankings? Can it capture the uncertainty and annotator disagreement present in preference data instead of discarding them? And since absolute quality judgments are expensive to annotate at scale while pairwise preference data is comparatively abundant, how can a reward model be grounded in an absolute quality scale using only limited quality annotations, for instance when adapting it to a new domain, without sacrificing ranking accuracy?

Paper type: Mostly experimental
Data type: Real-world data only
Experimental domains: LLM reward modeling for RLHF alignment, chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, code generation, chatbot safety, role-play dialogue

TITLE: Threshold transfer across domains for scalar and probabilistic reward heads
PROPOSAL: We test whether a single acceptance threshold keeps its meaning across domains. For a scalar Bradley-Terry head and for a probabilistic head that outputs a distribution over quality levels, both fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on the same pairwise data, we tune a threshold on absolute ratings from one domain and apply it unchanged to chat, mathematics, code and role-play candidates with held-out absolute ratings, measuring precision and recall of the accept decision in each domain and the drift of the score distribution of rated-good responses across domains.

COST: 240

TITLE: Pointwise probabilistic scoring against a generative judge at matched inference
PROPOSAL: Compare, at equal scoring work per candidate, a pointwise reward head that outputs a probability of acceptability with a generative judge that writes a critique before its verdict, both built on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and trained from the same pairwise data from UltraFeedback. Score candidate sets from a fixed policy on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark with N from two to sixty-four, select the best candidate under each scorer, and record the quality of the selection as judged by held-out human ratings and unit tests, together with the scoring latency and the accuracy of each scorer's own confidence about its verdict.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head, the generative judge with its critique removed, the generative judge with a critique length cap matching the pointwise head's latency, random selection as the floor, an oracle selection as the ceiling, and three seeds for training and for sampling candidates.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect the pointwise head to match the judge at small N and to pull ahead as N grows because the judge's pairwise format needs many comparisons. The judge should win on mathematics, where a critique catches wrong steps, and its advantage should vanish once its critique is capped.

TITLE: Evidential reward heads that flag inconsistent preference pairs
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head that outputs the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution over five quality levels, so that the model expresses both a quality estimate and how much evidence supports it, and we train it from pairwise data through the probability, under the Dirichlet, that the chosen response's expected level exceeds the rejected one's. We then use the evidence term to flag training pairs the model finds inconsistent, retrain after removing the flagged pairs, and measure whether ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench improves and whether the evidence term predicts annotator disagreement on HelpSteer2-Preference. Backbones are Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it, trained on Skywork-Reward-Preference.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head with and without the same fraction of pairs removed at random, removal based on the scalar head's loss instead of evidence, a Dirichlet head without the evidence regulariser, correlation of evidence with annotator split on held-out pairs, three seeds.
COST: 960
PREDICTION: We expect the evidence term to predict annotator split better than the scalar head's loss and the filtered retraining to gain a point or two of ranking accuracy on the chat subsets. Removing the same fraction at random should gain nothing, otherwise the gain is from data volume.

TITLE: Per-pair temperature from annotator disagreement in the pairwise loss
PROPOSAL: We modify the Bradley-Terry loss so that each pair has its own temperature, set from the recorded annotator agreement on that pair when available and otherwise predicted by a small auxiliary head trained on the pairs where it is available, so that contested pairs push the scores less than unanimous ones. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on HelpSteer2-Preference, which has per-pair agreement counts, and on Skywork-Reward-Preference, which has none, and we evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench, calibration of the sigmoid of score differences against held-out agreement, and whether a fixed threshold on scores separates responses by held-out absolute rating.
CONTROLS: Standard Bradley-Terry with a single temperature, the per-pair temperature set from a shuffled assignment of agreement counts as placebo, the auxiliary head alone as a predictor of disagreement, and three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect a small gain in ranking accuracy and a clear gain in calibration on the dataset with agreement counts, and a smaller transfer of both through the auxiliary head to the dataset without. The threshold test should show little change, because the temperature reshapes score differences and not the scale.

Problem statement:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a pivotal technique for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and intentions. As a critical component of this process, the reward model is trained to assign scores that quantify the degree of alignment between a model's outputs and human preferences. Well-designed reward signals, whether applied during training or at inference time (for example, to select the best among several sampled candidates), can significantly enhance LLM performance across diverse domains. However, learning a reward model that accurately captures human preference signals remains a significant challenge, and the two dominant paradigms both exhibit inherent limitations that hinder their effectiveness in practice.

Discriminative reward models append an MLP-based value head to a base model and are commonly optimized with the Bradley-Terry objective, which maximizes the score margin between chosen and rejected responses, to output a single scalar reward. Considerable research has improved this family through better data and refined modeling frameworks (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, and quantile- or uncertainty-based variants), yet these models remain limited to learning a pairwise ranking. Their scores are unbounded and uncalibrated, reflect only relative preferences rather than intrinsic quality, and lack a probabilistic interpretation: they indicate that one response is preferred over another, but not why, nor how good either response is in absolute terms. This makes it difficult to establish a trusted acceptance threshold that separates high-quality responses from low-quality ones. A single deterministic score per response also cannot express the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments: annotators often disagree, and inconsistent preference data is known to degrade reward model performance, yet such ambiguity is collapsed into a point estimate.

Generative reward models instead leverage the native generative capabilities of LLMs to produce chain-of-thought critiques before rendering a preference judgment, in line with the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, and recent reasoning-based variants trained with reinforcement learning show promising scalability in inference-time computation. While their critiques offer superior interpretability, they often rely on rigid pairwise input formats that limit flexibility in Best-of-N scenarios, where many candidates must be scored; they often struggle to outperform discriminative models under computational constraints; and achieving performance comparable to discriminative models frequently requires costly pointwise supervision for calibration, substantially increasing the annotation burden.

Consequently, the field faces a critical trade-off between the efficiency of discriminative reward models and the interpretability of generative ones, with neither offering a complete solution. This raises several open questions. Can a reward model match the efficiency and accuracy of discriminative models, score single or multiple responses flexibly, and still provide interpretable, calibrated scores with a meaningful measure of confidence? Can its scores reflect the absolute quality of a response, so that a fixed threshold reliably distinguishes good responses from bad ones, rather than encoding only relative rankings? Can it capture the uncertainty and annotator disagreement present in preference data instead of discarding them? And since absolute quality judgments are expensive to annotate at scale while pairwise preference data is comparatively abundant, how can a reward model be grounded in an absolute quality scale using only limited quality annotations, for instance when adapting it to a new domain, without sacrificing ranking accuracy?

Data type: Real-world data only
Experimental domains: LLM reward modeling for RLHF alignment, chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, code generation, chatbot safety, role-play dialogue

Problem statement:
Self-supervised contrastive learning has become a cornerstone paradigm for representation learning, enabling models to extract rich semantic features without explicit labels. At its core, contrastive learning constructs a latent space in which semantically similar samples (different augmented views of the same instance) converge while dissimilar samples diverge, and it is frequently guided by information-theoretic objectives such as maximizing the mutual information between views. Its empirical success has motivated extensive theoretical work: contrastive objectives have been decomposed into alignment and uniformity principles, related to mutual information maximization and noise contrastive estimation, and connected to spectral clustering on a data graph. Despite these advances, a fundamental tension persists between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. Existing analyses offer limited insight into the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process, in particular into how much new information the views presented to the model actually contribute for each individual instance.

In practice, current contrastive frameworks such as SimCLR, MoCo and their variants rely heavily on static, human-engineered augmentations and on large-batch sampling to enforce invariance and representational diversity. These choices impose rigid constraints on the learning dynamics: augmentations must balance semantic preservation against transformational complexity, while batch scaling faces unavoidable hardware limitations. Despite substantial engineering efforts to refine augmentation strategies, these methods fundamentally lack a principled mechanism for adaptively expanding the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence.

This leaves several open questions. How can the information gained through the views of an instance be characterized in a principled, information-theoretic way, so that augmentation design is guided by more than heuristics? Can the diversity of views be expanded adaptively and in a controlled manner, rather than only through fixed hand-crafted augmentation pipelines or ever larger batches, without sacrificing the semantic consistency that views of the same instance must share? And how should the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity be managed so that contrastive learning remains effective in small-batch, hardware-constrained settings?

TITLE: Per-instance view information gain estimated with a conditional entropy bound
PROPOSAL: We quantify, for each training image, how much a given augmented view adds beyond what the model already encodes, using a conditional entropy estimate computed from the embedding of the anchor and of the view under a small variational decoder trained alongside a SimCLR encoder. We train a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 with the standard augmentation set, log the per-instance gain for each augmentation family across training, and relate it to the final linear probe accuracy of the classes those instances belong to. TITLE: Feature-space view expansion gated by neighbourhood agreement at small batch
PROPOSAL: We generate additional positive views for each instance directly in the embedding space of a MoCo v2 encoder by moving the anchor embedding along directions sampled from the covariance of its nearest neighbours in the queue, and we admit a synthetic view only when its nearest-neighbour label agreement with the anchor, measured on a frozen copy of the encoder, stays above a threshold set on a validation split. Training runs on STL-10 and ImageNet-100 with a ResNet-50 at batch sizes of 64 and 256, and we evaluate linear probe and kNN accuracy as well as alignment and uniformity on the test set.
CONTROLS: The comparison includes the same encoder trained with image-space augmentations only at both batch sizes, the same encoder at batch 1024 as an upper reference point, synthetic views drawn along random isotropic directions of the same norm, and synthetic views admitted without the agreement gate, so that the contribution of the gate can be separated from that of the expansion itself.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Gated expansion should close most of the gap between batch 64 and batch 1024 on ImageNet-100 kNN accuracy, while ungated expansion should degrade alignment. If random directions perform as well as covariance directions, the neighbourhood structure is not what helps.

TITLE: Augmentation policy optimised against an information criterion rather than downstream accuracy
PROPOSAL: We learn an augmentation policy for SimCLR whose objective is a per-instance information criterion: the policy, a small network over augmentation magnitudes, is updated to maximise a variational lower bound on the mutual information between views while a semantic penalty, the disagreement between the two views under a frozen supervised classifier trained on a disjoint labelled split, is kept below a fixed level. TITLE: Small-batch contrastive learning with per-instance adaptive temperature driven by view agreement
PROPOSAL: We test whether the trade-off between invariance and expressivity can be managed per instance by setting the InfoNCE temperature of each anchor from the agreement between its views: anchors whose views already agree closely receive a lower temperature that sharpens separation from neighbours, while anchors whose views disagree receive a higher temperature that tolerates the spread. Agreement is the cosine similarity between view embeddings under a momentum encoder. We train ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 encoders on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-100 at batch sizes 32, 128 and 512 and measure linear probe accuracy, kNN accuracy, alignment and uniformity.
CONTROLS: A fixed temperature tuned per batch size, a global temperature schedule that decays over training, a temperature assigned from a shuffled agreement vector, and the same adaptive rule applied to a MoCo variant with a queue so that the effect is not specific to in-batch negatives, each over three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Adaptive temperature should help most at batch 32, narrowing the gap to batch 512 by roughly a third on ImageNet-100, and should give nothing at batch 512. If the shuffled assignment performs the same, the gain comes from the temperature distribution rather than from instance-level matching.

TITLE: A controlled synthetic benchmark for separating semantic invariance from view expressivity
PROPOSAL: We construct an image dataset from a rendering pipeline in which each instance has known semantic factors (object identity and shape) and known nuisance factors (pose, lighting, background and texture), so that for any augmentation the information shared between views and the information lost about each factor can be computed exactly from the generative model. COST: 150
PREDICTION: Linear probe accuracy on identity should rise and pose accuracy fall monotonically as the augmentation randomises more nuisance factors, with the crossing point predicted by the computed information quantities. The prediction fails if the exact quantities and the measured probe accuracies disagree on which augmentation setting is best, which would indicate that optimisation effects dominate the information picture.

TITLE: Replacing large batches with an instance-conditioned negative bank for hardware-constrained contrastive training
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the diversity usually obtained from large batches can be recovered by maintaining, for each instance, a small set of hard negatives selected by a momentum encoder from a queue and refreshed every epoch, so that each anchor sees a few informative negatives instead of thousands of random ones. We implement this on top of MoCo v2 with a ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100 and a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, with effective batch sizes of 32 and 64, and we compare representation quality by linear probe accuracy, kNN accuracy and the uniformity statistic, together with a measure of false negative rate using labels only at evaluation time.
CONTROLS: MoCo v2 with the standard queue at the same small batches, SimCLR at batch 1024 as the large-batch reference, the negative bank filled with random rather than selected negatives, and a variant where selection uses the online encoder instead of the momentum encoder.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Selected negatives should recover most of the kNN accuracy of the large-batch reference at batch 64, but the false negative rate should rise as selection becomes harder. We expect the random bank to perform no better than the standard queue.

Problem statement:
Self-supervised contrastive learning has become a cornerstone paradigm for representation learning, enabling models to extract rich semantic features without explicit labels. At its core, contrastive learning constructs a latent space in which semantically similar samples (different augmented views of the same instance) converge while dissimilar samples diverge, and it is frequently guided by information-theoretic objectives such as maximizing the mutual information between views. Its empirical success has motivated extensive theoretical work: contrastive objectives have been decomposed into alignment and uniformity principles, related to mutual information maximization and noise contrastive estimation, and connected to spectral clustering on a data graph. Despite these advances, a fundamental tension persists between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. Existing analyses offer limited insight into the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process, in particular into how much new information the views presented to the model actually contribute for each individual instance.

In practice, current contrastive frameworks such as SimCLR, MoCo and their variants rely heavily on static, human-engineered augmentations and on large-batch sampling to enforce invariance and representational diversity. These choices impose rigid constraints on the learning dynamics: augmentations must balance semantic preservation against transformational complexity, while batch scaling faces unavoidable hardware limitations. Despite substantial engineering efforts to refine augmentation strategies, these methods fundamentally lack a principled mechanism for adaptively expanding the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence.

This leaves several open questions. How can the information gained through the views of an instance be characterized in a principled, information-theoretic way, so that augmentation design is guided by more than heuristics? Can the diversity of views be expanded adaptively and in a controlled manner, rather than only through fixed hand-crafted augmentation pipelines or ever larger batches, without sacrificing the semantic consistency that views of the same instance must share? And how should the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity be managed so that contrastive learning remains effective in small-batch, hardware-constrained settings?

TITLE: Does the augmentation graph spectrum tell us when more views stop helping
PROPOSAL: We examine the claim that contrastive learning performs spectral clustering on an augmentation graph by measuring, on real datasets, how the spectrum of the empirical augmentation kernel changes as augmentation strength increases, and whether the eigenvalue decay predicts the information that further views add. TITLE: Diffusion-generated views under a per-instance semantic distance target for small-batch SimCLR
PROPOSAL: We expand the set of views per instance with samples from a class-agnostic image diffusion model conditioned on the anchor through an image-to-image process with noise strength chosen per instance. The noise strength is raised until the cosine similarity between anchor and generated view under a frozen pretrained encoder drops to a target level, so that every instance receives views of comparable semantic distance rather than comparable pixel distortion. We train SimCLR with a ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100 at batch sizes 64 and 256, mixing one generated view with one standard view per instance, and evaluate linear probe and kNN accuracy, alignment and uniformity, and transfer to CIFAR-100.
CONTROLS: Standard augmentations alone at both batch sizes and at batch 2048, generated views at a fixed noise strength for all instances, generated views from an unconditioned diffusion sample matched to the anchor only by class, and views produced by strong hand-crafted augmentation tuned to the same average similarity, three seeds each.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Per-instance noise strength should outperform fixed strength and should narrow the gap between batch 64 and batch 2048 by about half. Class-matched unconditioned samples should hurt alignment, confirming that the gain needs instance-level conditioning.

TITLE: View scheduling from running per-instance information estimates
PROPOSAL: We allocate the number of augmented views drawn per instance in each epoch according to a running estimate of how much its recent views disagreed in embedding space, giving more views to instances whose views still carry fresh information and fewer to instances whose views have converged. The estimate is the exponential moving average of the per-instance InfoNCE loss computed under a momentum encoder. We train BYOL and SimCLR with ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet with a fixed total number of views per epoch equal to the standard two views per instance, so that the scheduler redistributes work rather than adding it, at batch sizes 64 and 256.
CONTROLS: Uniform two views per instance, allocation by a random score with the same histogram, allocation by the inverse of the score to check the direction of the effect, and allocation by class-level rather than instance-level averages.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Instance-level scheduling should improve linear probe accuracy by about one point on Tiny-ImageNet at batch 64 and less at batch 256. If the inverse allocation performs equally, the loss signal does not track view informativeness.

Problem statement:
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP learn to align visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space, enabling effective performance on a wide range of multi-modal tasks such as image classification, multi-modal retrieval and semantic segmentation. The introduction of natural language gives VLMs better flexibility and generalization than traditional visual classification models. To further enhance their performance, numerous training-time approaches, such as prompt learning from labeled data, have been proposed, introducing effective optimization solutions and inference paradigms.

In contrast to training-time approaches, test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have attracted increasing attention for their ability to enhance the performance of VLMs during inference without requiring additional annotated data. Depending on the type of test data, TTA methods can be broadly categorized into episodic and online strategies. Episodic TTA adapts the model to a single test sample, exploring the information inside that sample to improve the model's prediction. Online TTA processes a stream of test data, using historical knowledge from previously seen samples to update model behavior. A growing number of methods of both kinds have been proposed, each typically reporting gains over earlier ones.

However, existing TTA research for VLMs suffers from various limitations in experimental setup and analysis. First, most works rely on reported baseline results without reproducing them under consistent experimental settings. This leads to unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts and evaluation protocols, so it is unclear how much of the reported progress reflects genuine algorithmic improvement. Second, except for a few works that explore alternative evaluation metrics, the majority of research focuses narrowly on accuracy, resulting in an incomplete understanding of what adaptation does to a model, even though real-world deployment requires models that are also reliable and robust. Third, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time and on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, which limits the generalizability of existing conclusions. Together, these problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

This raises several open questions. When existing episodic and online TTA methods are compared under consistent and controlled conditions, how much do they actually improve over the unadapted model, and how much real progress have recent methods made over the earliest ones? Do their gains generalize to VLMs other than CLIP, and does test-time adaptation complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of the model? Finally, beyond classification accuracy, does accuracy-oriented test-time adaptation preserve or compromise the trustworthiness and stability that practitioners need for reliable deployment?

TITLE: What test-time adaptation does to calibration, selective prediction and shift detection
PROPOSAL: We measure, beyond accuracy, what adaptation does to the reliability of CLIP ViT-B/16 predictions: expected calibration error, negative log-likelihood, area under the risk-coverage curve for selective prediction, and the AUROC of maximum softmax probability for separating ImageNet from ImageNet-O as an out-of-distribution detection task. Methods are TPT, C-TPT, MTA, TDA and DPE, run on ImageNet, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R and the fine-grained datasets. We report every metric before and after adaptation for the same test images, so that each method is characterised by a vector of changes rather than a single accuracy delta.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model, temperature scaling of the unadapted model fitted on a held-out split as a calibration-only baseline, each method with its confidence-selection step disabled, and three stream orders for the online methods.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: Entropy-minimising methods should lower calibration error on the shifted sets while raising it on in-domain ImageNet, and the risk-coverage area should improve less than accuracy does. If temperature scaling alone matches the calibration changes, the adaptation adds nothing to reliability beyond a confidence rescaling.

TITLE: Stability of online test-time adaptation under stream order and label shift
PROPOSAL: We test whether online methods for CLIP keep their accuracy when the test stream changes character: we run TDA, DMN, DPE and BoostAdapter on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch and the fine-grained datasets under four stream regimes, a random order, a class-sorted order, a stream with a sudden switch between two datasets, and a stream that repeats a small subset many times. We record accuracy over the stream in windows of 500 samples and calculate the variance of windowed accuracy and the worst window for each method. We also measure how fast each method recovers after the dataset switch.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model, each episodic method as an order-independent reference, each online method with its cache reset every window, and five random orders to bound the variance expected from sampling alone.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: Cache-based methods should lose several points under class-sorted streams and recover slowly after a switch, while episodic methods stay flat. If resetting the cache every window removes the loss, the instability sits in cache contents rather than in the update rule.

Problem statement:
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP learn to align visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space, enabling effective performance on a wide range of multi-modal tasks such as image classification, multi-modal retrieval and semantic segmentation. The introduction of natural language gives VLMs better flexibility and generalization than traditional visual classification models. To further enhance their performance, numerous training-time approaches, such as prompt learning from labeled data, have been proposed, introducing effective optimization solutions and inference paradigms.

In contrast to training-time approaches, test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have attracted increasing attention for their ability to enhance the performance of VLMs during inference without requiring additional annotated data. Depending on the type of test data, TTA methods can be broadly categorized into episodic and online strategies. Episodic TTA adapts the model to a single test sample, exploring the information inside that sample to improve the model's prediction. Online TTA processes a stream of test data, using historical knowledge from previously seen samples to update model behavior. A growing number of methods of both kinds have been proposed, each typically reporting gains over earlier ones.

However, existing TTA research for VLMs suffers from various limitations in experimental setup and analysis. First, most works rely on reported baseline results without reproducing them under consistent experimental settings. This leads to unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts and evaluation protocols, so it is unclear how much of the reported progress reflects genuine algorithmic improvement. Second, except for a few works that explore alternative evaluation metrics, the majority of research focuses narrowly on accuracy, resulting in an incomplete understanding of what adaptation does to a model, even though real-world deployment requires models that are also reliable and robust. Third, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time and on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, which limits the generalizability of existing conclusions. Together, these problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

This raises several open questions. When existing episodic and online TTA methods are compared under consistent and controlled conditions, how much do they actually improve over the unadapted model, and how much real progress have recent methods made over the earliest ones? Do their gains generalize to VLMs other than CLIP, and does test-time adaptation complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of the model? Finally, beyond classification accuracy, does accuracy-oriented test-time adaptation preserve or compromise the trustworthiness and stability that practitioners need for reliable deployment?

TITLE: Does entropy minimisation help on reliability, a metric-by-metric audit of TPT descendants
PROPOSAL: We take the family of episodic methods built on entropy minimisation over augmented views, TPT, DiffTPT, C-TPT and RLCF, and audit each on CLIP ViT-B/16 with a panel of reliability metrics: expected calibration error, Brier score, prediction consistency across augmentations, and the fraction of test images whose predicted class flips between the unadapted and adapted model. COST: 110
PREDICTION: Flip fractions should exceed the net accuracy gain by a factor of three or more, meaning methods swap many predictions to gain a few. If the random-view variant matches the confidence-selected one, the selection step is not what drives the gain.

TITLE: Replaying the adaptation literature in order to measure cumulative progress
PROPOSAL: We arrange ten test-time adaptation methods for CLIP in order of their appearance, from TPT to the most recent online method, and run each under the same harness on ViT-B/16 with the same prompts on ImageNet, its shift variants and the fine-grained datasets. We then plot the accuracy of each method against its position in the sequence and fit a piecewise-linear trend, which gives the cumulative gain over the first method and the gain of each method over its immediate predecessor under equal conditions. We repeat the plot for the gains each paper printed to compare the two trends.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model as the origin of both curves, each method also run with its own paper's checkpoint and prompt, and three stream orders for the online methods.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: The printed trend should rise steadily while the equal-conditions trend should flatten after the first two online methods. If the two trends agree, protocol variation has not contributed to the reported progress.
