Problem statement:
Visual synthesis has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the scaling of Transformer architectures. Video generation in particular has attracted growing interest from both academia and industry, owing to its wide-ranging applications in content creation, world simulation and beyond. At present, diffusion models lead the field by iteratively denoising latent representations to produce high-fidelity clips. Concurrently, autoregressive models have been explored for their potential to unify image and video generation and to generalize over longer time horizons.

Despite their successes, each paradigm exhibits critical shortcomings. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing fixed-length frame sequences by exploiting bidirectional attention, yet they incur substantial computational cost due to tens or even hundreds of sequential denoising steps, and they struggle to extend seamlessly to video extrapolation; their slow generation speed hinders the production of high-resolution, long-duration videos. Autoregressive methods based on next-token prediction, which predict video tokens in a fixed order (for example token by token along both spatial and temporal axes, as in Emu3, or set by set in space and then frame by frame in time, as in Nova), are inherently capable of streaming generation, but they often fall short in visual fidelity and require hundreds to tens of thousands of inference steps, resulting in prohibitive latency.

These observations motivate the need for a generation framework that simultaneously possesses high visual quality, efficiency and temporal generalization. In image synthesis, Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR) recently redefined generation as a coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction, and its follow-up, Infinity, introduced bitwise modeling and scaled up the vocabulary size, achieving performance comparable to diffusion models while offering significant advantages in inference speed. These advances, however, concern the spatial-only generation of static images. Whether a discrete autoregressive approach can deliver comparable quality and speed for video, where the temporal dimension, far larger token counts and the need for coherent motion come into play, remains an open question.

Several obstacles make this difficult. Discrete video tokenizers, on which purely discrete generators depend, are usually either trained from scratch, which is computationally heavy for clips of tens of frames and converges slowly, or initialized from discrete image tokenizers, whose weights are not optimal for video reconstruction. Long videos also imply long contexts: maintaining temporal consistency requires attending to previously generated content, yet attending to the full history leads to explosively long sequences and high computational cost.

The problem is therefore to design a single, purely discrete autoregressive model that generates high-resolution (e.g., 720p) videos with visual quality competitive with leading diffusion models at much lower inference latency, while unifying text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation within one framework, and extending to long, multi-round video generation that follows successive user instructions. How should the temporal dimension be modeled so that a single model serves both images and videos and faithfully captures both appearance and motion? How can discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality be obtained without prohibitive training cost? And how can the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts be contained without sacrificing temporal consistency or visual quality?

Paper type: Experimental only
Data type: Mostly real-world data
Experimental domains: text-to-video generation, text-to-image generation, image-to-video generation, video extrapolation, long interactive video generation

TITLE: Scale-then-frame next-scale prediction for unified image and video generation
PROPOSAL: We extend Infinity-style bitwise next-scale prediction to video by treating each frame as a sequence of scales, ordering tokens scale-major within a frame and frame-major across time, so that an image is a one-frame video and the same model handles text-to-image, text-to-video and image-to-video by changing only the conditioning prefix. We train a 2B-parameter transformer on a mix of image-text pairs and 5-second clips at 480p, then adapt it to 720p with a short second stage.
CONTROLS: Baselines: a diffusion transformer of matched size trained on the same clips, an Emu3-style token-by-token raster model, and a frame-major variant that predicts all scales of frame t only after completing frame t-1. Ablations: scale-major against frame-major ordering, bitwise against index prediction, and the image share of the data mix at two levels.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Scale-major ordering within a frame should reach VBench scores within a few points of the diffusion baseline at under a tenth of its latency and beat the raster model on FVD on UCF-101. If motion smoothness lags far behind the diffusion model, the within-frame scale ordering is breaking temporal coupling and the frame-major variant should then win.

TITLE: Obtaining a discrete video tokenizer by temporal expansion of an image tokenizer
PROPOSAL: We take the bitwise image tokenizer of Infinity, replace each 2D convolution by a causal 3D convolution whose central temporal slice carries the image weights and whose other slices start at zero, and fine-tune only the temporal slices and the quantizer on 17-frame clips at 256p before unfreezing everything briefly at 480p. CONTROLS: We compare against the same architecture trained from scratch on the same clips, against a tokenizer with the image weights copied into every temporal slice, and against the plain 2D tokenizer applied frame by frame. TITLE: Coarse-scale history for long video generation with bounded context
PROPOSAL: We give the generator a context made of the last four frames at every scale plus only the two coarsest scales of all earlier frames, so that the attended sequence grows slowly while global layout and identity remain visible. Training randomises the cut-off so the model learns to work with any history length, and we optimise for the generation of two-minute videos at 480p in rounds of eight seconds, each conditioned on a new instruction.
CONTROLS: Full-history attention up to the length that fits, a pure sliding window of four frames without any coarse history, a window that keeps only the first frame as anchor, and a key-value cache compressed by token merging at equal memory. We measure subject consistency and background consistency on VBench-Long, drift of CLIP similarity to the first frame over time, and per-frame latency as the video lengthens, over three seeds.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Coarse-scale history should hold subject consistency within a few points of full attention while keeping per-frame latency flat, and beat the plain sliding window by a wide gap on background consistency. Failure would show up as the model ignoring the coarse history, in which case the first-frame anchor would match it.

TITLE: Multi-round instruction-following video extension in one discrete model
PROPOSAL: We train the unified next-scale generator with a conversational format in which each round appends a text instruction and a continuation of forty-eight frames conditioned on the whole previous video through compressed history. Training clips are cut into segments with per-segment captions produced by a captioning model, so that the generator sees instruction changes in the middle of a video. We evaluate five-round generations in which each instruction changes the camera motion or an object action.
CONTROLS: A single-round model asked to regenerate the whole video with the concatenated instructions, a diffusion extension baseline that continues from the last frames only, and our model with the history truncated to the current round. Metrics: per-round instruction adherence judged by a vision-language model and checked by two raters, subject consistency across rounds, and the share of rounds in which motion follows the new instruction.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Round-by-round generation should follow new instructions in most rounds while keeping subject identity across rounds, and the diffusion extension baseline should drift on identity after the third round. The likely failure is that the generator ignores late instructions and continues the previous motion, which the adherence metric would show as a drop after round two.

PROPOSAL: We compare three ways of placing time inside next-scale prediction: spatiotemporal pyramids where each scale is a coarser video cube, per-frame scale pyramids ordered frame by frame, and per-frame pyramids predicting the residual against the previous frame at each scale. TITLE: Bitwise vocabulary scaling for video tokens
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the bitwise prediction that lets Infinity grow its image vocabulary carries over to video tokens, where motion adds entropy. We train tokenisers with 16, 24 and 32 bits per token and generators that predict each bit with an independent sigmoid head, and we measure reconstruction and generation at 480p on Kinetics-600 and on a web-video corpus with captions.

COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect generation FVD to improve from 16 to 24 bits and to flatten at 32, with the gap to rFVD widening as bits grow. If the autoregressive-within-token variant beats independent bits by a wide gap, bit independence is the wrong assumption for motion.

TITLE: Spatiotemporal attention patterns that keep long contexts affordable
PROPOSAL: We replace full attention in the video generator with structured patterns and measure quality against context length: within-frame full attention plus attention to the same spatial block in previous frames, attention to previous frames only at the coarsest scale, and a learned selection of the most relevant previous-frame tokens per query. Discrete video tokenizers, on which purely discrete generators depend, are usually either trained from scratch, which is computationally heavy for clips of tens of frames and converges slowly, or initialized from discrete image tokenizers, whose weights are not optimal for video reconstruction. Long videos also imply long contexts: maintaining temporal consistency requires attending to previously generated content, yet attending to the full history leads to explosively long sequences and high computational cost.

The problem is therefore to design a single, purely discrete autoregressive model that generates high-resolution (e.g., 720p) videos with visual quality competitive with leading diffusion models at much lower inference latency, while unifying text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation within one framework, and extending to long, multi-round video generation that follows successive user instructions. How should the temporal dimension be modeled so that a single model serves both images and videos and faithfully captures both appearance and motion? How can discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality be obtained without prohibitive training cost? And how can the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts be contained without sacrificing temporal consistency or visual quality?

Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning, but the way they use such newly injected knowledge is puzzling. On the one hand, recent work showed that LLMs are able to deduce implications from learned facts: a model that learns the new fact "Alice lives in Paris" during fine-tuning can generalize at test time to deduce "Alice speaks French", an implication of the injected fact given that people living in Paris speak French. This indicates strong generalization capabilities. On the other hand, other work shows that LLMs tend to hallucinate factually incorrect responses when they learn new factual knowledge during fine-tuning. It remains unclear why LLMs can be good at generalization yet prone to hallucination after being injected with new factual knowledge. This raises a natural question: do generalization and hallucination on newly injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?

A capability closely related to this question is out-of-context reasoning, also referred to as "ripple effects": a model's ability to deduce implications beyond the explicitly trained knowledge by drawing connections between different pieces of knowledge. Prior studies of this capability in LLMs paint a mixed picture. Negative results have been reported on certain out-of-context reasoning tasks, such as the reversal curse and multi-hop in-weight reasoning, while other work shows that LLMs can associate two events when several subjects are involved in both events in the training data. Formally, atomic knowledge can be written as triples (s, r, a), where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer. An underlying rule may link facts to implications, so that any subject s having relation r_1 with answer b_i also has relation r_2 with answer c_i; for example, (s, lives in, Paris) implies (s, speaks, French). Suppose a model is trained on data in which some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication. If a new subject appears during training only in the fact, can the model deduce the unseen implication at test time? And how, if at all, does this capability relate to the hallucinations observed after knowledge injection?

A rigorous understanding of this behavior is still lacking. The mechanism by which LLMs associate such events has so far been analyzed only empirically. A growing body of theoretical work explains how transformers acquire reasoning behaviors, such as induction heads, factual recall, the reversal curse, chain-of-thought reasoning and in-context two-hop reasoning, by studying their training dynamics. Yet it is not understood how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, which properties of the model and of its training make this possible, and under which conditions on the training data it occurs. Answering these questions would help explain both the strong generalization of LLMs after knowledge injection and their tendency to hallucinate, and could make it possible to predict when hallucination arises as new factual knowledge is injected into a model.

Paper type: Mostly theoretical
Data type: Mostly synthetic data
Experimental domains: factual knowledge injection in LLMs, open-domain question answering

PROPOSAL: We build a synthetic corpus of triples where each subject has a fact relation r1 with answer b and, for a fraction of subjects, the implied relation r2 with answer c under a fixed rule from b to c. TITLE: Training dynamics of implication transfer in a simplified transformer
PROPOSAL: We analyse gradient flow for a one-layer transformer with a single attention head followed by a two-layer MLP, trained with cross-entropy on synthetic triples under a rule from r1 answers to r2 answers, with orthogonal subject embeddings. We aim to prove that the MLP learns a map from the b answer direction to the c answer direction that is shared across subjects, and that this map transfers to a subject trained only on its r1 fact because the attention head writes the subject's b direction into the residual stream at the r2 query. We derive the time at which transfer appears as a function of the number of bridging subjects and the embedding dimension.
CONTROLS: Numerical simulation of the same model at dimensions 64, 256 and 1024 to check the predicted transfer time, a model without the MLP that should fail to transfer, and a 125M model trained on the same corpus to see whether the derived scaling holds beyond the simplified setting.
COST: 24
PREDICTION: Transfer time should scale inversely with the number of bridging subjects and the simulation should match the theory within a constant factor. The theory could fail if the attention head learns a subject-specific rather than a relation-level pattern, which the 125M model would reveal.

Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning, but the way they use such newly injected knowledge is puzzling. On the one hand, recent work showed that LLMs are able to deduce implications from learned facts: a model that learns the new fact "Alice lives in Paris" during fine-tuning can generalize at test time to deduce "Alice speaks French", an implication of the injected fact given that people living in Paris speak French. This indicates strong generalization capabilities. On the other hand, other work shows that LLMs tend to hallucinate factually incorrect responses when they learn new factual knowledge during fine-tuning. It remains unclear why LLMs can be good at generalization yet prone to hallucination after being injected with new factual knowledge. This raises a natural question: do generalization and hallucination on newly injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?

A capability closely related to this question is out-of-context reasoning, also referred to as "ripple effects": a model's ability to deduce implications beyond the explicitly trained knowledge by drawing connections between different pieces of knowledge. Prior studies of this capability in LLMs paint a mixed picture. Negative results have been reported on certain out-of-context reasoning tasks, such as the reversal curse and multi-hop in-weight reasoning, while other work shows that LLMs can associate two events when several subjects are involved in both events in the training data. Formally, atomic knowledge can be written as triples (s, r, a), where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer. An underlying rule may link facts to implications, so that any subject s having relation r_1 with answer b_i also has relation r_2 with answer c_i; for example, (s, lives in, Paris) implies (s, speaks, French). Suppose a model is trained on data in which some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication. If a new subject appears during training only in the fact, can the model deduce the unseen implication at test time? And how, if at all, does this capability relate to the hallucinations observed after knowledge injection?

A rigorous understanding of this behavior is still lacking. The mechanism by which LLMs associate such events has so far been analyzed only empirically. A growing body of theoretical work explains how transformers acquire reasoning behaviors, such as induction heads, factual recall, the reversal curse, chain-of-thought reasoning and in-context two-hop reasoning, by studying their training dynamics. Yet it is not understood how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, which properties of the model and of its training make this possible, and under which conditions on the training data it occurs. Answering these questions would help explain both the strong generalization of LLMs after knowledge injection and their tendency to hallucinate, and could make it possible to predict when hallucination arises as new factual knowledge is injected into a model.

Paper type: Mostly theoretical
Data type: Mostly synthetic data
Experimental domains: factual knowledge injection in LLMs, open-domain question answering

TITLE: Knowledge injection into pretrained models: deduction and hallucination on fictional entities
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Llama-3-8B and Pythia-1.4B with low-rank adapters on 2000 facts about fictional people, each stating that a person lives in a real city, and we test whether the models deduce the language, currency and continent implied by the city for people never shown with those implications, while measuring hallucination as confident answers to questions about attributes that the facts never determine, such as the person's profession.

We report deduction accuracy, hallucination rate at several confidence thresholds, and their correlation across checkpoints over three seeds.

PREDICTION: Deduction accuracy and hallucination rate should climb together across checkpoints, and the scrambled-city condition should remove deduction while leaving some hallucination. If hallucination stays flat while deduction rises, the two have separate sources.

TITLE: Data conditions under which implication transfer appears
PROPOSAL: We map the region of training-data parameters in which a transformer trained from scratch on synthetic triples deduces unseen implications: the number of bridging subjects per rule, the number of distinct answers b, the ratio of fact to implication sentences, and the share of rule-violating subjects. Each point of the grid trains a four-layer 30M-parameter transformer and we fit a phase boundary in this space.
CONTROLS: The same grid for a model trained with the implication sentences placed before the facts in each document, a grid with subjects replaced by random tokens at test time, a memorisation baseline that scores answers by co-occurrence counts, and three seeds per grid point with the boundary refitted on each seed.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Transfer should switch on when bridging subjects exceed a threshold that falls as distinct answers grow, and rule violations above a small share should erase it. The co-occurrence baseline matching the model anywhere in the grid would show that deduction there is spurious.

TITLE: Predicting hallucination before injecting a fact
PROPOSAL: We compute, before fine-tuning on a new fact about a subject, a score that reads the alignment between the model's representation of the fact answer b and the learned rule map from r1 answers to r2 answers, and we test whether this score predicts which subjects will receive wrong implications after injection. TITLE: Scaling of implication transfer with width, depth and data
PROPOSAL: Train transformers of 10M, 30M, 100M and 300M parameters from scratch on synthetic triples with ten rules and measure, for each, the number of bridging subjects needed before held-out implications are deduced, along with the hallucination rate on subjects whose fact lies outside every rule. Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning, but the way they use such newly injected knowledge is puzzling. On the one hand, recent work showed that LLMs are able to deduce implications from learned facts: a model that learns the new fact "Alice lives in Paris" during fine-tuning can generalize at test time to deduce "Alice speaks French", an implication of the injected fact given that people living in Paris speak French. This indicates strong generalization capabilities. On the other hand, other work shows that LLMs tend to hallucinate factually incorrect responses when they learn new factual knowledge during fine-tuning. It remains unclear why LLMs can be good at generalization yet prone to hallucination after being injected with new factual knowledge. This raises a natural question: do generalization and hallucination on newly injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?

A capability closely related to this question is out-of-context reasoning, also referred to as "ripple effects": a model's ability to deduce implications beyond the explicitly trained knowledge by drawing connections between different pieces of knowledge. Prior studies of this capability in LLMs paint a mixed picture. Negative results have been reported on certain out-of-context reasoning tasks, such as the reversal curse and multi-hop in-weight reasoning, while other work shows that LLMs can associate two events when several subjects are involved in both events in the training data. Formally, atomic knowledge can be written as triples (s, r, a), where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer. An underlying rule may link facts to implications, so that any subject s having relation r_1 with answer b_i also has relation r_2 with answer c_i; for example, (s, lives in, Paris) implies (s, speaks, French). Suppose a model is trained on data in which some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication. If a new subject appears during training only in the fact, can the model deduce the unseen implication at test time? And how, if at all, does this capability relate to the hallucinations observed after knowledge injection?

A rigorous understanding of this behavior is still lacking. The mechanism by which LLMs associate such events has so far been analyzed only empirically. A growing body of theoretical work explains how transformers acquire reasoning behaviors, such as induction heads, factual recall, the reversal curse, chain-of-thought reasoning and in-context two-hop reasoning, by studying their training dynamics. Yet it is not understood how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, which properties of the model and of its training make this possible, and under which conditions on the training data it occurs. Answering these questions would help explain both the strong generalization of LLMs after knowledge injection and their tendency to hallucinate, and could make it possible to predict when hallucination arises as new factual knowledge is injected into a model.

Paper type: Mostly theoretical
Data type: Mostly synthetic data
Experimental domains: factual knowledge injection in LLMs, open-domain question answering
